summary:
Surviving on Mars is an interactive resource-management and space-survival video game designed for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Inspired by the gameplay of 60 Seconds!, the player must gather key supplies before starting a 12-sol mission on the Martian surface.

The project tackles the challenge by turning the real constraints of a space outpost into tangible engineering decisions for kids ages 7 to 12. Every sol, players receive a limited energy budget that they must distribute strategically among four critical areas: Life Support, Greenhouse, Shield, and Science. Along the way they face random events that raise the difficulty and force them to weigh real trade-offs, such as sacrificing food production to strengthen radiation protection.

This tool matters because it sparks an early interest in science careers, letting kids experience, in a fun and educational way, the real challenges astronauts face in deep space.
details:
Project Details

What exactly does it do?

Surviving on Mars is an interactive strategy and resource-management video game designed so that kids ages 7 to 12 can experience the real challenges of operating an outpost on Mars during a 12-sol mission. The game translates real space-engineering constraints, such as energy scarcity, life support, food production, and radiation protection, into playful decision-making mechanics.

How does it work?

The Surviving on Mars experience is divided into two main phases:

  • Collection phase: Before the mission begins, the player has a limited amount of time to select and gather the critical supplies and tools to take to the Martian base.
  • Survival phase (12 sols): Once on Mars, the player receives a limited energy budget every sol (day) and must distribute it strategically among four essential modules: Life Support, Greenhouse, Shield, and Science. As the sols go by, dynamic events (such as solar storms, equipment failures, or environmental fluctuations) raise the difficulty and force the player to weigh real trade-offs: no decision is free, and prioritizing one area means taking on risk in another.

What benefits does it have?

  • Active learning: It teaches critical thinking, risk management, and real space-exploration concepts without relying on long theoretical texts.
  • Accessibility: Its intuitive interface and dynamic gameplay let kids ages 7 to 12 understand the complexity of space missions in an entertaining way.
  • Replayability: The combination of starting items collected and progressive events creates different scenarios in every playthrough.

What do you hope to achieve?

We aim to spark an interest in science and technology careers from an early age, helping young players understand the real constraints of survival in deep space and appreciate the work of astronauts and space-mission engineers.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • React 19 + Vite
  • Three.js + react-three/fiber + react-three/drei: handled all the 3D
  • Zustand: handled the game state
  • Framer Motion: handled the interface animations and transitions
  • Textures are generated by code; there are no external images except the characters and the cabin illustrations.
  • All images in the game were created with Gemini.

How is your project creative?

Surviving on Mars takes the formula of a race-against-the-clock survival game, in the style of 60 Seconds!, and brings it to a space mission for kids. Instead of explaining space weather with text, it turns it into something the player has to face: the solar storms in the game are real coronal mass ejections from NASA’s DONKI database, with their actual date and speed, and they hit on the day the simulation predicted they would reach Mars.

It is also creative in how it shows consequences. The base changes with the player’s decisions: an ignored leak keeps losing air, and an ice mine or a newly built panel stays and helps until the end. On top of that, emergencies are not solved from a menu alone: the commander walks out into the base and fixes them by hand, sealing a crack, cleaning panels, or reconnecting wires, while crewmates guide the player and ask for help. Decisions are made on a retro-style computer that prints a ticket with the outcome before confirming, so the child sees the effect of each choice.

What factors did your team consider?

  • The audience’s age: the game is designed for kids ages 7 to 12, with a cadet mode for ages 9 and under (more time, fewer events, and a suggested option) and a harder game for older players.
  • Accessibility: read-aloud narration, large text, the full game in English and Spanish, and controls that work with a mouse, a keyboard, or a touchscreen.
  • Available devices: it runs in the browser with nothing to install, adapts to computers, tablets, and phones, and has a light mode for older devices.
  • Scientific honesty: we use real NASA data and explain inside the game what we simplified. With no connection, the game uses saved real data and says so.
  • Privacy: the player’s name and age stay in the browser; they are never stored or sent.
  • Game balance: we tuned the difficulty with simulated playthroughs and player testing, so that no fixed strategy always wins and losing invites another try.
